 Millions on Disability Could Get a Bigger Social Security Check in 2027 - Here's Why
 Estimates point to the largest COLA in four years.
 By
 Josh Koebert 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Oct. 25, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.

For the roughly 8 million Americans receiving Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI), the annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is not a retirement plan variable to optimize. It is the difference between keeping up with rising expenses and falling further behind. 
The official 2027 COLA is the largest increase SSDI beneficiaries have seen since 2023, and it comes with a few important details worth understanding before January arrives.

 The official 2027 COLA is 3.6%
 The Social Security Administration officially announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027 on October 14, 2026. The increase applies to Social Security retirement and disability benefits beginning in January 2027.
 The adjustment is calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) for July, August, and September, compared with the same period the previous year.
 The final figure came in close to earlier forecasts from organizations including the Senior Citizens League and AARP.
 At 3.6%, the 2027 COLA is the largest since 2023, when beneficiaries received an 8.7% increase. The 2026 COLA was 2.8%.

 How the COLA works on an individual check
The adjustment applies as a percentage to whatever your individual benefit amount is, not as a flat dollar figure added to every check. 
That means the dollar increase varies from person to person. According to the SSA, the average disabled worker's benefit is expected to increase from $1,642 to $1,701 per month in January 2027, a gain of approximately $59 per month under the official 3.6% COLA. 
Someone receiving a higher benefit, say $2,000 per month, would see a proportionally larger dollar increase: about $72 per month at 3.6%. 
The adjusted amount takes effect with the January 2027 payment. Personalized COLA notices go out from the SSA in December, and beneficiaries can also log into their my Social Security account at ssa.gov to see their new amount before the January check arrives. 
 The Medicare offset that shrinks the actual gain
For disability beneficiaries who are enrolled in Medicare, the headline COLA percentage is not the same as the increase in the amount deposited into their account. 
Medicare Part B premiums are deducted directly from Social Security checks for most enrollees. The 2026 Part B premium is $202.90 per month. The 2027 Part B premium will be announced separately in the fall, typically in November, and projections suggest another increase is likely. 
If the monthly Part B premium rises by $10 to $15 in 2027, a beneficiary who gained $55 from the COLA would net out closer to $40 to $45 after the premium increase is deducted. The raise is still meaningful. It is just smaller than the percentage figure suggests when the Medicare cost is factored in. 
Beneficiaries who are not yet enrolled in Medicare, particularly those under 65 who qualified for SSDI on the basis of disability, receive the full COLA increase without this offset.

 The SSDI-specific thresholds that also move with the COLA
The COLA does not just change monthly benefit amounts. It also adjusts several work-related thresholds that are particularly important for SSDI beneficiaries who are working or considering returning to work. 
Substantial gainful activity (SGA) 
 The SGA limit is the monthly earnings amount above which the SSA considers a person capable of substantial work, which can end SSDI eligibility. For 2026, the SGA limit is $1,690 per month for non-blind individuals and $2,830 per month for those who are statutorily blind. In 2027, those limits increase to $1,770 and $2,950 per month, respectively. These amounts are indexed to the national average wage index and adjusted each year alongside the broader COLA cycle. 
Trial work period (TWP) threshold 
 The TWP allows SSDI beneficiaries to test their ability to work for up to nine months without immediately losing benefits, regardless of how much they earn during those months. A month counts as a trial work month when earnings reach or exceed $1,210 in 2026. That threshold increases to $1,270 in 2027. That threshold also adjusts annually. 
The SSA announced the updated 2027 thresholds alongside the official COLA on October 14, 2026. For beneficiaries navigating work incentives, knowing these updated thresholds in advance helps with planning. 
 The persistent criticism of the CPI-W
Every year the COLA is announced, the same objection follows: The CPI-W is the wrong measuring stick. 
The CPI-W tracks spending patterns of urban wage earners and clerical workers, meaning it reflects what working-age people buy and how prices affect them. Disabled individuals and older adults spend a significantly larger share of their income on health care and housing, both of which have historically risen faster than the overall inflation rate the CPI-W captures. 
The Bureau of Labor Statistics produces a separate index called the CPI-E, specifically designed to track inflation as experienced by Americans aged 62 and older. The CPI-E consistently runs higher than the CPI-W. 
 Advocacy organizations including the Senior Citizens League have pushed for years to have Social Security COLAs calculated using the CPI-E instead, arguing that the current method systematically underestimates the inflation that disability and retirement beneficiaries actually face. 
The Senior Citizens League's 2026 Loss of Buying Power study found that Social Security benefits have lost roughly 14% of their purchasing power since 2016 even with annual adjustments, because those adjustments consistently lag behind what beneficiaries actually spend. No legislation switching to the CPI-E has passed. 
 Bottom line
The official 2027 Social Security COLA is 3.6%, giving SSDI recipients their largest raise since 2023. According to the SSA, the average disabled worker's monthly benefit will increase by approximately $59, before any Medicare premium increases. 
To see how the adjustment could affect your benefits for seniors or disability payments, visit ssa.gov. You can review your benefit amount and access your official COLA notice once it's available.
